notes.title: Game Update: Bunny Optimization + Mesh Merge
notes.notes:
No need to open if you're an old player — no gameplay changes.
I've refactored part of the bunny code and merged their meshes to improve performance.

------------------------------
I reduced the number of skinned meshes, and the game runs faster now.
It was a painful and tedious process, but I did learn some new things.
Maybe the next game will be better because of it.
I’m honestly afraid all three of my games will get the same kind of comments — that would make it seem like I haven’t improved at all over the years.

------------------------------

Performance Stats
Before (initial version):
• Visible skinned meshes: 298
• Animator components playing: 250

After converting flower animation from bone-based to shader vertex animation:
• Visible skinned meshes: 152
• Animator components playing: 208

After today's bunny mesh merge:
• Visible skinned meshes: 91
• Animator components playing: 43

------------------------------

I finally merged the bunny meshes. And then I remembered why I didn’t do it before.

Having a bunch of scattered small mesh parts is terrible for runtime efficiency,
but it’s great for development — quick to iterate.
Once the mesh is merged, every small adjustment (weighting issues, modeling errors, export problems, adding a new accessory, etc.) requires re-assigning all 25+ materials from scratch.
After doing that a few times, I nearly lost my mind — groundhog screaming noises included.
But screaming doesn’t help, so I kept dragging materials.

Eventually, I thought of numbering the materials to make reassigning them in order easier.

Also, exporting directly from Blender to Unity sometimes just... fails.
Now I export the FBX manually, then drag it into Unity.
Even with numbered materials, doing this over and over is frustrating.
Then I discovered something: if I delete the old FBX but keep its `.meta` file, and reimport a new FBX with the same filename, Unity keeps the material assignments.

No idea why I hadn’t thought of that earlier.
It reminded me of how, as a kid, Chinese homework, when I had to copy homework twice, I’d hold two pens and write both at the same time.
Turns out lots of classmates did that too — or used carbon paper.
Experienced devs are just better at skipping unnecessary steps.

------------------------------

Development is Pain

Some bugs are systemic — they only stop biting you once you’ve been bitten a few times.
Even if I switched engines or 3D software, I’d just run into different bugs.
You just get better at dodging them with time.

------------------------------

I still remember waiting forever for my game’s first ever review.
The player was nice and gave it a positive rating,
but also mentioned the game was poorly optimized.
(Later they deleted the review — maybe they were worried it would hurt my feelings?)

Back then, I had no idea what "optimization" meant.
None of the “anyone can make a game” tutorials talked about it.

3 years later, I think I finally understand what that comment meant.

------------------------------

For example:

• I modeled the bunny and exported it as-is. If it worked, great.
• I didn’t think ahead — now that there are tons of bunny outfits, I can’t even tell which file was the original.
• I threw materials into the scene however I liked.
Now there are hundreds of them scattered around.
Trying to optimize textures and reduce draw calls now is a huge task.

I hope I can avoid all this next time.

---

What’s Next
I want to rewrite the bunny system with a more efficient architecture…
but I don’t know how yet.
I’ve started watching some video tutorials — hopefully I’ll get there.

------------------------------
That'all for chatting. Thanks for being my playper.

The following is for chatting, no need to read-------------------

I've been busy with my new game recently, repeatedly making demos and then scrapping them multiple times. 
After nearly reaching the breaking point, I finally found inspiration for the new game!! 
Now I'm happily continuing the development. 
The new game focuses more on storytelling and reduces the animation parts, making the overall art aspect more manageable. 
That's about it. It's really nice to finally have some progress to show. 
It was truly frustrating when I had to keep revising and scrapping previous ideas, leaving progress at zero.

notes.title: Update some UI, changed some filters, add bubbles for horse, fixed some bugs
notes.notes:
Updates:
Changed startup page.
Added tooltips to UI elements when the mouse hovers over them.
Added bubbles following the horses.

Bug Fixes:
Addressed a bunch of minor bugs.
Modified the filter for the firefly scene.
Restored the fence that was previously removed.

—————— You don’t need to read anything below. That's just for chatting:——————

After each refactoring, the code becomes more concise. Simplicity takes time. Writing messy code is quicker but less efficient.

Lately, I've been reading "Software Testing," 2nd Edition by Ron Patton. 
section 3.1.4 humorously states, "The more software defects found, the more software defects exist." Haha, quite amusing. 
It's fortunate that these bugs were found when the user base was still small and within my fixable scope. 

Occasionally, I look at the differences between the first, second, and third games of independent game developers. Some stick to a similar style, while others show clear evolutionary changes in their games.

Restored the fence that was removed. Initially, it was deleted because it was causing bunnies to get stuck in their paths. I adjusted some parameters, so bunnies shouldn't get stuck, and I added it back.

A joke I came across: "Those in our profession must not fall in love with customers. Never remember the names of customers; otherwise, you'll be very sad later." — A web writer.

In the early stages of creation, with very few users, many creators would go read all user comments, even memorize their avatars and IDs. Later on, when users started looking at new works and playing new games, creators felt really sad. 

Recently, I'm trying to implement a feature I find interesting. 
It feels like I'm constantly jumping between "What I want to do" and "What I'm technically capable of doing." 

Well, that's all. 
Thank for reading.

notes.title: Fixed bugs, removed some item, update UI
notes.notes:
If you've already played this game, there's no need to play this version. 
I just removed some items, fixed bugs, didn't add new features. 
Play when new features are added next time.

Update:
* Moved the controls to the main page.
* Separated the game settings UI from the gameplay interface logic.
* Fixed a bunch of other bugs, mainly encountered by new players with saves.
* Fixed the issue where birds/horses get stuck when helping with harvesting.
* Removed fog. I saw players encountering black screen issues again. It was caused by volumetric fog before, I couldn't figure out the specific reason, so I just turned off the entire fog.
* Removed the sound played by the rabbit's TV.


You don’t need to read anything below. That's just for chatting:
---------------------------------------------------------------------

This time, there's a massive removal. 
For instance, the adorable little pig is no more, farewell little pig ⊂((・x・))⊃. 
Bunny In Black has vanished as well. 
Perhaps they'll make a comeback later, maybe not; I haven't decided yet. 
It's a bit sad, isn't it? 
The pig spaceship is super cute, the pig is cute too, and I invested a lot of effort in making the pig automatically gaze at the bunny's IK part.

I'm planning to delete this segment first and then introduce new features.

Deleting features is quite troublesome, especially dealing with the mountain of garbage code—like attempting to replace a doorknob and the entire house collapses with a bang. 
But... remember, I've refactored the code several times~ So, when I delete the code, although it's challenging, I can carve out a bloody path.

Then this time, all saved game files were deleted, and I discovered some new bugs, which only trigger for new players. 
No wonder there are suddenly no new comments... 
New players don't complain, they just quietly close the game or request a refund. 
Just fixed it... sad howling... If only I had known earlier...

If I had enough money, I would hire someone to play my game every morning and night, then provide me with feedback on bugs... 
No, wait, when I have money, I can hire smart people to code, so I won't have to fight with bugs.

During development, I've played it countless times. I read a game book talked about when developers are too familiar with their own game, making it hard to understand the confusion players face. 
I am busy with a new game for a while, reopened this game recently, looked at it with fresh eyes, found a lot of problematic areas. So fixed it again.

notes.title: Update UI, Fixed some bugs (horse, bird AI bug) etc.
notes.notes:
This is a small UI update to fix some bugs and do minor refactoring. 
(You don't need to read the following, it's just for communication purposes.)

-------------------------------------------------------------------------
Although the code has been rewritten, users may not notice a big difference on the front end.

Lately, I've been thinking about adding a storyline feature, but I was planning to wait for major feature improvements before writing an update. 
That's why I didn't initially want to write update notes, as I was afraid people would think the author is nagging.

There was a period in between when I didn't do anything and just lay down watching dramas. I watched one series multiple times and then switched to another. Watched it several times too.
I thought I was experiencing procrastination or being lazy.
The process of making a game is too tough. It exhausted me like crazy.
I didn't realize it until after lying down for a while and slowly recovering.

Indeed, I once thought that if I had money, I would lead others to make games while I focus on creativity. That would probably make me happy.
But then I saw an interview with Director Kong Dashan(Journey to the West 2021), and it seems that even when you have the money and people, it's still tough. 
In the end, independent games and movies are equally challenging processes.

Making major changes to the game is too expensive. Every time I'm passionate about the artistic part, when I come back to the implementation part, reality slaps me in the face.

Of course, it's still much better than making a movie. They have to find funding, actors, arrange locations, deal with weather, special effects, and so on.
So I don't have much to complain about. If the game doesn't make money, it's just not making money, and it's only my personal time invested. But if a movie loses money, the stakes are much higher.
Yes, that's how I console myself.

Recently, there was a group of reviewers who played my game, and I was quite moved.
Some people were especially kind and even provided screen recordings, which was a huge help.

Because I'm the only one making the game, many times when players describe UI issues with text, I can only guess the solution. Because I'm too familiar with the game, everything seems like the correct operation to me.
I couldn't understand what players meant when they said "the text is overlapping" because it appeared normal on my computer.
But after watching their videos, I discovered some bugs that had never occurred on my computer. Once I saw them, I understood where the bugs were and knew how to fix them.

Many games rely on player support to keep going. I'm also very grateful for your encouragement.
Many times, I also felt that my game wasn't good enough, and I thought about giving up and going back to a regular job. Your positive feedback has given me more motivation.

As for the storyline part of the game, I'm currently learning the coding part.
Hahahaha... Yes, this is my first game, and there are many things I need to learn how to do before implementing them in the game.

That's about it.
Thank you for always following me  (＾ｰ^)ノ

notes.title: Refactored code, update night scenes, and some UI
notes.notes:
Thank you for your sincere message. 
I was also a bit surprised to see that people are actually paying attention to the updates. 
I often wait a long time for a new message and sometimes worry that I'm just talking to the air.

Getting feedback is a pleasant surprise, especially when someone points out specific issues in the game. It shows that someone is actually playing it! 
I'm so happy about that! My first reaction was to climb onto the roof and shout, "Someone is playing my game!" 
But... I have to fix the bugs and continue writing code first.

Game design is fun, but the implementation process is painful and time-consuming. 
I design happily, but then I have a furrowed brow when it comes to implementation.

For this update, I updated some UI and added night lighting to some of the buildings.
I also refactored part of the code. 
This was a painful and time-consuming process, but it was worth it. 

I don't know if you guys play Jenga or not. 
As a novice game designer (like me), I often just write functions directly, like making the bunny run, sleep, eat, and so on. Gradually, the unstable blocks pile up higher and higher. 
Players may not realize it, but I know that the project is about to collapse. 

So I have to stop and spend a lot of time refactoring the code. Although players can't see the difference, they can see the new features that have been added. 

Finally, the refactoring is done. I played it myself and didn't encounter any bugs. 
This was a big change, so there may be some overlooked bugs that I didn't find during testing. Please leave a message and let me know. 

Thank you.
